trial_name: SMART — Balanced Crystalloids vs Saline in Critically Ill Adults (2018)
citation: Semler MW, Self WH, Wanderer JP, et al; SMART Investigators and Pragmatic Critical Care Research Group. Balanced crystalloids versus saline in critically ill adults. N Engl J Med. 2018;378(9):829-839.
one_liner: In a pragmatic ICU trial, default balanced crystalloids modestly reduced MAKE30 compared with saline (14.3% vs 15.4%; OR 0.90; P=0.04).

pico.population: Adults admitted to five ICUs at a single academic centre.
pico.intervention: Unit-level default to balanced crystalloids (lactated Ringer's or Plasma-Lyte A) for isotonic crystalloid orders.
pico.outcome: Major Adverse Kidney Events within 30 days (MAKE30: death, new RRT, or persistent renal dysfunction).

background.existing_knowledge: 0.9% saline was the dominant ICU crystalloid despite supraphysiological chloride; balanced crystalloids more closely match plasma chloride and include buffer anions, potentially reducing hyperchloraemic acidosis and renal vasoconstriction.
background.knowledge_gap: Uncertainty whether fluid chloride load affects patient-centred outcomes (kidney failure, survival).
background.hypothesis: Balanced crystalloids would reduce MAKE30 compared with saline when delivered early and pragmatically.

methods.design: Pragmatic, cluster-randomised, multiple-crossover trial embedded in routine care; single academic centre; five adult ICUs; unit-level monthly fluid assignment.
methods.setting: Five adult ICUs (medical, cardiac, neurological, trauma, surgical) at Vanderbilt University Medical Center, June 2015 to April 2017.

inclusion: All adults (≥18 years) admitted to participating ICUs.
exclusion: None for enrolment; clinician override permitted; for kidney components, patients with pre-existing RRT before ICU admission were ineligible for new RRT and persistent renal dysfunction criteria (but remained eligible for mortality).

methods.intervention: Unit-level default to balanced crystalloids (predominantly lactated Ringer's; Plasma-Lyte A available) for IV isotonic crystalloids (bolus and maintenance). Electronic order sets and stocking aligned to deliver assigned fluid early.
methods.comparison: Unit-level default to 0.9% saline for IV isotonic crystalloids.
methods.blinding: Unblinded (clinicians aware of monthly assignment); outcomes largely objective and EHR-derived.
methods.sample_size_power: 14,000 ICU admissions planned to detect 1.9% absolute reduction in MAKE30 (15.0% to 13.1%) with 90% power at two-sided 5% alpha.
methods.primary_outcome: MAKE30: composite of in-hospital death before day 30, new RRT, or final creatinine ≥200% of baseline (censored at day 30/discharge).
methods.follow_up: Primary outcome through hospital discharge or 30 days; mortality also at 60 days; organ support-free days through day 28.

headline_bullets: MAKE30: 14.3% balanced vs 15.4% saline (adjusted OR 0.90, 95% CI 0.82–0.99, P=0.04)
Individual components directionally consistent but not individually significant
Sepsis subgroup: MAKE30 33.8% vs 38.9% (OR 0.80, 95% CI 0.67–0.94, interaction P=0.06)
Less hyperchloraemia with balanced crystalloids (24.5% vs 35.6%)

outcomes_table.note: Composite of in-hospital death (censored at day 30), new RRT, or final creatinine ≥200% baseline

subgroup_table.subgroup: Sepsis or septic shock at ICU admission

safety: No signal of increased hyperkalaemia with balanced crystalloids

domains.notes: Cluster randomisation at ICU-month level with repeated crossovers; allocation unconcealed due to overt default strategy.
Open-label; primary outcome used objective endpoints (death, creatinine, RRT) reducing detection bias, but RRT initiation clinician-mediated and susceptible to expectation bias.
Pragmatic all-comers enrolment; 15,802 ICU admissions among 13,949 unique patients; sensitivity analysis restricted to first ICU admission attenuated primary effect (not statistically significant).
High adherence: assigned fluid accounted for 93.4% of isotonic crystalloid orders in balanced months vs 97.8% in saline months; clear separation in fluid exposure.
Groups closely matched (age, sex, mechanical ventilation, vasopressors, sepsis, predicted mortality).
Death and RRT complete; creatinine-based outcomes required baseline creatinine imputation; sensitivity analyses showed dependence on creatinine handling.
Analyses accounted for clustering/crossover with prespecified covariate adjustment; primary P=0.04, modest, with interim monitoring.

internal_validity.verdict: Internal validity moderate to strong: pragmatic enrolment and objective endpoints support robustness; limitations include open-label, single-centre, clinician-mediated RRT, and creatinine imputation sensitivity.

domains.notes: Broad adult ICU case-mix across five specialised units, minimal exclusions, pragmatic delivery; relevant to many mixed medical-surgical ICUs.

Single-centre; results may depend on local practice patterns (baseline fluid choice, RRT thresholds, ED/OR alignment). Neurocritical care and TBI may require tailored strategies. Highly implementable where EHR defaults and supply chain can enforce unit-level assignment; resource-limited settings may differ.

external_validity.verdict: Generalisability good for adult mixed ICUs in high-resource systems, limited by single-centre nature and dependence on local RRT practices and pre-ICU fluid exposure.

strengths: Very large pragmatic ICU trial; minimal exclusion and default strategy design reduced selection bias
High protocol adherence with strong separation
Rapid translation potential via EHR defaults
Paired with ED companion trial (SALT-ED) enabling broader inference
limitations: Cluster-multiple-crossover design can introduce time-varying confounding
Primary effect size modest and driven by composite with non-significant components
RRT initiation susceptible to clinician discretion
Creatinine-based components depend on baseline/last creatinine measurement and imputation
Balanced crystalloids comprised more than one formulation without head-to-head randomisation

critical_appraisal.summary: SMART demonstrated a modest reduction in MAKE30 with balanced crystalloids, supported by strong pragmatic design and clear physiological separation, but limited by single-centre, open-label design and sensitivity of composite endpoint components.
strengths: High protocol adherence and clear fluid separation
EHR-embedded default strategy enabling rapid translation
weaknesses: Modest effect size with non-significant individual components

sections.authors_conclusion: Using balanced crystalloids as the ICU default produced a modest reduction in MAKE30 compared with saline, supporting balanced crystalloids as a reasonable default isotonic crystalloid for many critically ill adults, especially where kidney injury prevention is prioritised.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: Balanced crystalloids are a reasonable default ICU crystalloid, offering a small reduction in MAKE30, but the absolute benefit is modest and may be context-dependent.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: Adult mixed medical-surgical ICU patients, particularly those with sepsis or high fluid volumes; caution in traumatic brain injury.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: Balanced crystalloids are not proven to reduce mortality or RRT individually; the benefit is driven by a composite endpoint.
implementation_caveats: Single-centre results; local RRT practices and pre-ICU fluid exposure may influence effect
EHR default implementation may be needed to achieve similar adherence
Later multicentre trials did not replicate mortality benefit, suggesting benefit may be smaller or subgroup-specific

controversies.notes: NEJM editorial interpreted SMART alongside SALT-ED, emphasising patient-centred outcomes and pragmatic value while noting small effect sizes and endpoint choice matters.
MAKE30 is clinically meaningful but composite; primary signal emerged despite non-significant individual components, raising interpretability questions.
Strength (system default with minimal exclusions) is also a limitation (unblinded, centre-specific pathways), increasing importance of replication.
Larger apparent benefit in sepsis/septic shock (MAKE30 OR 0.80; interaction P=0.06) is biologically plausible but hypothesis-generating given multiplicity.
BaSICS (JAMA 2021) and PLUS (NEJM 2022) did not show overall mortality benefit, suggesting benefit may be smaller, context-specific, or subgroup-dependent.
FLUID trial (NEJM 2025; ~159,000 patients) found no clear difference in death/readmission composite (20.3% LR vs 21.4% saline; adjusted difference −1.1 pp; 95% CI −2.4 to 0.2).

NEJM Evidence 2022 meta-analysis estimated small mortality benefit (RR 0.96; 95% CrI 0.93–0.99; posterior probability of reduced mortality ~89.5%), but absolute effect small and heterogeneity by population (e.g., TBI) remains.
Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021 suggested balanced crystalloids over saline for initial resuscitation in sepsis/septic shock, reflecting aggregate evidence.
ESICM 2024 clinical practice guideline on fluid therapy (Part 1) synthesised post-SMART evidence and provides updated framework for selecting resuscitation crystalloids.

context_related_trials.relation: Companion ED trial; together suggested benefit across acuity settings.
Multicentre ICU trial (JAMA 2021) with neutral primary mortality outcome.
Multicentre ICU trial (NEJM 2022) with neutral primary mortality outcome.
Hospital-wide crossover trial (NEJM 2025) with no clear difference in death/readmission composite.
Estimated small mortality benefit (RR 0.96) but with heterogeneity and small absolute effect.

unresolved_questions: Whether balanced crystalloids confer a mortality benefit in specific subgroups (e.g., sepsis) remains uncertain.
Optimal fluid choice in traumatic brain injury requires further study.
The role of balanced crystalloids in resource-limited settings is unclear.

quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: Default balanced crystalloids in the ICU modestly reduce MAKE30, supporting their use as a reasonable default, but later trials suggest any mortality benefit is small and context-dependent.
